To compute a sup distance, maximize the absolute difference over the entire function domain,
not only at fixed sample points. Another equivalent metric on R is d(x, y) = |x − y|/(1 + |x − y|):
balls of radius r < 1 are ordinary intervals of radius r/(1 − r), and the whole space is bounded in
d. Thus equivalent topologies can have different bounded sets.

question.text:
Which function is a metric on R?
(A) d(x, y) = 0 for every x, y
2
(B) d(x, y) = (x − y)
(C) d(x, y) = |x + y|
(D) d(x, y) = |x − y| − 1
(E) d(x, y) = min{1, |x − y|}

solution.text:
Truncation at one preserves the triangle inequality because min(1, a + b) ≤ min(1, a) +
min(1, b). The other choices violate the triangle inequality, zero-distance condition, or
nonnegativity.

question.text:
For the metric d(x, y) = |x − y|/(1 + |x − y|) on R, what is B (0, 1/2), and is the whole space
d
bounded in this metric?
(A) (−1, 1); yes (B) [−1, 1]; yes (C) (−1, 1); no (D) (−1/2, 1/2); yes (E) R; yes

solution.text:
The strict inequality |x|/(1 +|x|) < 1/2 is equivalent to |x| < 1. Every distance in this metric
is less than one, so the whole space is bounded. More generally, for 0 < r < 1 the metric
ball is an ordinary interval of radius r/(1 − r), so the metric still induces the usual topology;
boundedness is not determined by topology alone.
